Silence here is an inconsistency in practice at the one place it matters.

primary_reviews.rationale: The quoted Hebrew is accurate. The problem is the sentence the whole span rests on: 'None of the internal seams (16/17/18/19/20) carry a distinct speech or scene marker.' That fails at the very first internal seam. Verse 16 has bene Qeini as its subject; v17 opens wayyelekh Yehudah et Shim'on achiw, an explicit new subject that also resumes the Judah-Simeon pairing introduced at 1:3. Under the criterion this campaign applies at 1:21 and at 4:11, an explicit-subject participant change is a seam. The same syntactic signal is thus treated as a unit-opener in ch4 and as invisible in ch1. The medium_low rating partially discloses the softness but does not repair the false premise, and the rejected alternative examined (splitting v20) tests the weakest of the five internal seams rather than the strongest.

primary_reviews.rationale: Quotes verify and both marker claims (pe after 1.29, pe after 1.36) are correct against the file. The span's outer edges are also right. But the decision turns on the register-closure criterion, and it applies that criterion on a factual premise the text contradicts. The rationale states the entries share the 'X didn't drive out the inhabitants of Y' formula 'without any discrete per-entry closure device.' In fact every entry terminates in a repeated closure clause of the dwelling / forced-labour / non-dispossession type: Manasseh (27-28) closes wayyo'el ha-Kena'ani lashevet ba-aretz ha-zot and then we-horesh lo horisho; Ephraim (29) wayyeshev ha-Kena'ani be-qirbo be-Gazer; Zebulun (30) wayyihyu la-mas; Asher (31-32) ki lo horisho; Naphtali (33) hayu lahem la-mas; Dan/Amorite (34-35) wayyihyu la-mas. That is six entries, six terminal closure clauses. Under the criterion as stated to me - uniform registers whole, but discrete per-entry closure decisive - the evidence points the other way once the clauses are counted. Independently, four samekh sites (1.28, 1.30, 1.32, 1.33) plus the disclosed pe at 1.29 land on five of the six entry-ends; that is weak corroboration only and cannot drive, but it is undisclosed and it converges with the closure clauses. I am not asserting the register must be split; I am asserting the stated ground for keeping it whole is not available as written.

primary_reviews.rationale: Both Hebrew lines verify and the boundary itself is probably right - but not for the first reason given. The rationale names the opening driver a 'fresh anger-formula.' It is not fresh. Wayyichar af YHWH be-Yisra'el occurs verbatim in consonants and vowels at 2:14, six verses earlier and inside the immediately preceding span, and again at 3:8 inside the Othniel span, where this campaign rightly treats it as span-internal. So the formula recurs three times in the range and opens a unit exactly once. The explicit-subject formula-reset principle forbids a repeated formula from opening a unit without a subject reset or a content shift; the subject is YHWH in all three occurrences, so no reset is available and the whole weight must fall on the content shift the rationale also cites - third-person description giving way to first-person divine speech introduced by wayyomer ya'an asher. That ground is sound and I accept it. What I cannot accept is a rationale that presents a thrice-used formula as though its appearance were itself the signal, because that reasoning, generalised, would open units at 2:14 and 3:8 as well.

primary_reviews.rationale: Directly answers Focus Test 3. Checked vv7-11 line by line: there is no scene-setting, no dialogue, no place name beyond Aram-Naharaim, and no named locality anywhere in the five verses -- nothing but the framework formulas themselves (sin, servitude, cry, raise, Spirit, victory, rest-and-death). That is the correct explanation for why this cycle collapses into one span while Ehud's does not: Othniel's story simply is the formula, with no narrative content available to subdivide, whereas Ehud's cycle has the same formula plus an extensive narrative interior. The rejected alternative (folding all of 2:6-3:11 together) is properly declined on a checkable description-versus-instantiation distinction between 2:11's iterative verbs and 3:7's terser one-time report. High confidence is earned by both edges (first-instance formula opening, rest-and-death-plus-samekh closing).

Both parashah corrections check out against the two-witness file: pe does fall after 3:11, and chapter 3's setumot are confined to 3:14, 3:30 and 3:31, so the earlier samekh attribution was wrong and the fix is right. The HIGH grade is earned at both edges rather than asserted. On the left, 3:6 terminates the nations register with a pe of its own and 3:7 begins narrating a named deliverance instead of describing a pattern; on the right, 3:11 carries the pe and 3:12 reopens with wayyosifu, 'again,' which is the formula's own signal that a fresh cycle is starting. The cycle-close family rule this row is made to anchor is coherent as stated and survives testing against the two other configurations it governs: 3:11 stays absorbed because the rest-notice and the death notice share one clause-chain inside a five-verse unit that is formula throughout with nothing to peel it away from, 3:30 stands alone undiluted, and 5:31 is forced into a poem's closing stanza by verse granularity. Three textual situations, one policy, applied without contradiction.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: OL's mechanical correction is right: parashah_two_witness.json lists Judg.3.11 among the 65 pe sites, not the 27 samekh sites, and ch3's samekh entries are 3.14, 3.30, and 3.31 only. The marker should read 'pe after Judg.3.11,' with no effect on confidence since Prophets marks are weak corroboration regardless of type. On the larger campaign-wide question this decision anchors (whether the cycle-close formula is treated consistently at 3:11, 3:30, and 5:31): 3:11 absorbs Othniel's close because the whole five-verse unit is formula with no separable narrative to peel it from, and the rationale says so explicitly; 3:30 (M8-Judg-020) isolates Ehud's close as its own decision because Ehud's cycle does have substantial separable narrative -- preparation, assassination, escape, battle -- once that narrative exists, the close can be and is peeled off; 5:31 (M8-Judg-039) absorbs the Song's rest-formula for a third, independent reason: verse-level granularity physically prevents separating the poetic couplet from the prose notice within one verse. The three outcomes (absorbed, isolated, absorbed) rest on two distinct and individually defensible principles -- 'no separable content to split from' and 'granularity forbids separation' -- rather than one rule applied inconsistently, but the campaign has never stated this as a single explicit policy, which is what invites the appearance of inconsistency. I recommend adopting and cross-referencing one stated rule: isolate the closing formula whenever it can be separated from preceding narrative without violating verse granularity, and disclose the specific reason (no separable content, or granularity) whenever it is instead absorbed.

primary_reviews.rationale: Hebrew verifies. What the rationale calls a scene-narrowing is, in the syntax, a disjunctive clause: we-Ehud ba elaw fronts the subject before the verb, and it is answered four verses later by another fronted subject, we-hu yatza at 3:24. So this span sits between two syntactically marked disjunctions, which is a firmer basis than the prose description suggests. The cast reduction is real too - only Ehud and Eglon appear across 20-23, and the servants do not enter until 24. Closing on the locking of the doors rather than on the flight keeps the concealment with the killing, which the text supports since wayyisgor ... we-na'al completes the action begun in v21. Medium under-rates a span whose both edges carry fronted-subject clauses, but I do not challenge conservative ratings.

primary_reviews.rationale: Quotes verify exactly and the participant-narrowing at v20 plus the concealment action at v23 are real, checkable scene markers. My objection is comparative rather than local to this span. This is one of six consecutive decisions (015-016 then 017-020) that carve Ehud's tribute-to-death-to-flight-to-battle sequence into separate beats, while the campaign treats the structurally parallel doublet -- Jael's hospitality-ruse-then-killing-then-discovery at 4:17-22 -- as a single span (see decision 028). Both are 'trusted private approach ends in the enemy commander's death by an unexpected hand' type-scenes that commentators regularly read as a matched pair; under a type-scene-grammar lens the two ought to get comparable granularity, or the asymmetry should be argued for on its own terms (for instance, that Ehud's scene is bracketed by cyclical framework formulas that Jael's is not). As currently written, decision 017-020 and decision 028 never cross-reference each other, so the six-way split here looks like an artifact of how the material happened to be worked through rather than a stated literary judgment.

challenges.claim: Ehud's assassination-and-aftermath sequence (roughly 3:16-3:27, spanning decisions 016-018) is split into three or more separately-bounded beats, while the parallel deceptive-private-killing type-scene at 4:17-22 (Jael and Sisera, decision 028) is kept as a single span, with no stated rationale for the difference in granularity between the two doublets.
challenges.suggested_action: Either reconcile the granularity between Ehud's assassination complex and Jael's (e.g., by consolidating 3:20-23/3:24-27 the way 4:17-22 is consolidated, or by splitting 4:17-22 the way Ehud's scene is split), or add an explicit note explaining why the two type-scenes warrant different treatment.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: LF's comparative point is fair but identifies an undisclosed asymmetry with a real textual basis rather than a plain error. Ehud's complex (3:16-30) is subdivided at four separate formula/scene resets -- object-making (016), the cast-narrowing to just Ehud and Eglon (this span), the servants' delay-and-discovery with its own Wiederaufnahme (018), and Ehud's battle-summons speech-act (019) -- each independently marked. Jael's complex (4:17-22) has no comparable internal speech-act or formula reset between the opening flight and Barak's arrival; it runs as one continuous action sequence without a dialogue interruption until the end. That is a textually grounded reason the two doublets could reasonably receive different granularity, but LF is right that neither decision states this, and an explicit cross-reference explaining the asymmetry, rather than silence, would strengthen both.

primary_reviews.rationale: Both quotations verify. The closing edge is fine - we-lo nimlat ish is a terminal notice and v30 shifts into summary register. The opening edge is where this decision fails its own rulebook. 3:27 ends we-hu lifnehem with Ehud as subject; 3:28 opens wayyomer alehem, a wayyiqtol speech formula carrying no explicit subject at all and referring to that same Ehud, inside an unbroken consecutive chain that runs from the trumpet blast through the descent to the summons. The explicit-subject formula-reset principle permits a repeated speech formula to open a unit only where a subject reset or a content shift supplies the break. Neither is present: the subject is not restated, and blowing the shofar to muster the tribes and then telling the muster to follow is one continuous military action, not two registers. Compare the openers this campaign accepts elsewhere - 1:3 wayyomer Yehudah le-Shim'on and 4:14 wattomer Devorah el Barak - both carry the explicit subject the principle demands. The rationale's ground, that this is Ehud's 'first recorded speech to the muster rather than to Eglon,' is an observation about addressee within one scene, not a marked seam.

challenges.claim: The span opens on wayyomer alehem at 3:28 - a speech formula with no explicit subject, referring to the same actor as 3:27, inside a continuous wayyiqtol chain. Under the explicit-subject formula-reset principle this cannot open a unit without a subject reset or content shift, and neither is supplied; the campaign's own accepted openers at 1:3 and 4:14 both carry explicit subjects.
challenges.suggested_action: Either merge 3:28-29 into the preceding muster unit (3:24-27), or retain the split and re-argue the opening on a signal the text supplies other than the subject-less speech formula; if retained, disclose that the opener fails the explicit-subject test and lower confidence accordingly.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: OL is right on the mechanics: 3:27 ends with the pronoun-only ve-hu lifnehem, and 3:28's vayyomer alehem carries no explicit subject at all, referring back to the same Ehud across an unbroken wayyiqtol chain, confirmed against Judg_oshb.txt. That fails the explicit-subject formula-reset test as stated and cited against 1:3 and 4:14, both of which carry explicit subjects. Where I would push back slightly: this campaign's practice elsewhere shows addressee change can open a unit independently of an explicit-subject reset, and 3:28 does mark a genuine addressee shift -- Ehud's first recorded speech to the muster rather than to Eglon -- which is a real signal even without a restated subject. I would resolve this by disclosing that the opener fails the strict subject-reset test while resting the boundary on the addressee shift instead, rather than merging into 3:24-27 or leaving the gap unaddressed.

OL supplies something more, though: the epithet YHWH Elohei Yisrael closes both v3 (azammer la-YHWH Elohei Yisrael) and v5 (mipne YHWH Elohei Yisrael), and I confirmed by scanning the chapter that these are its only two occurrences in the Song -- a genuine lexical refrain-bracket, which is a driver-list signal, not metadata. That bracket argues v3 belongs with the theophany (4-5) rather than with v2's summons, putting the real strophic seam between v2 and v3 rather than between v3 and v4 as currently drawn across 031/032. I support both challenges' factual claims -- the \b marks and the epithet bracket are both real -- but the \b evidence alone should not move the boundary; the epithet bracket is the one piece of admissible corroboration here, and it argues for a different split than either challenge explicitly proposes (v2 alone, then v3-5), which the campaign should engage directly.

primary_reviews.rationale: The citations verify, and the dated opener bi-yme Shamgar ben Anat bi-yme Ya'el is a genuine registral marker. The closing edge is where this fails, and it fails twice over. First, the rationale rejects extending to v11 on the ground that v9 'reintroduces the first-person' against 'the third-person historical description of 6-8.' Verse 7 is not third-person: it carries shaqqamti twice, a first-person suffix conjugation form, and WEB renders it accordingly ('until I, Deborah, arose; until I arose a mother in Israel'). The register contrast the decision relies on therefore does not exist at the point where it is needed, since first-person address is already inside 6-8. Second, I mapped every blank-poetry-line strophe divider in WEB's Judges 5 - they fall after verses 2, 3, 5, 9, 11, 12, 18, 23, 27, 30 and 31 - and this span's close at v8 is the only Song span-close in the whole chapter that does not land on one. The nearest divider is after v9, which is precisely where the rejected alternative would have put the seam. So the sole boundary in ch5 lacking lineation support is also the one whose stated ground is contradicted by the morphology.

primary_reviews.rationale: The falsification is correct and the withdrawal is unavoidable: shaqqamti stands twice in v7, so no contrast between third-person description in 6-8 and first-person in 9-11 can survive, whatever one decides about whether the ending is archaic second feminine or first common singular. Disclosing that the poem's own lineation runs 6 through 9 unbroken, with the next divider only after v9, is honest and correctly weighted as non-driving. Worth adding rather than challenging: v9's ha-mitnaddevim ba'am ... barakhu YHWH recycles v2's be-hitnaddev am ... barakhu YHWH, so v9 opens by refrain, which supplies the independent strophe-opening signal the row currently rests on mood alone. Neither point disturbs the seam under review, since nothing falls at v8 either way.

Naming that as a third category and saying why is better practice than stretching a rule to cover a case it was not built for. The description fix is also right: Gideon is named at first mention in 6:11, so the earlier 'unnamed farmer' had to go. One thing the row leaves on the table rather than gets wrong — pe falls after 6:6 and again after 6:10, and the translation opens a paragraph at 6:7, so both of this span's edges carry weak corroboration that goes uncited. Medium is therefore a conservative grade rather than a stretched one. The 6:11 citation differs from the stored line in three accents, which does not touch the argument.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: LF's mechanical correction is confirmed directly: 6:11's own text names Gideon at first mention (ve-Gid'on beno chovet chittim), so 'unnamed farmer' in the rejected-alternative note is simply inaccurate; the collective-versus-individual argument does not depend on the naming detail and needs no other change. On OL's Wiederaufnahme point: 6:7's wayehi ki za'aqu bene Yisra'el el YHWH does closely echo 6:6's vayyiz'aku bene Yisra'el el YHWH, and the campaign should state which precedent governs rather than leaving it silent. But there is a distinction OL's own framing elides: at 3:26 and 4:17, the resumption backs the narrative up over an intervening verse to resume a suspended thread; here 6:6 and 6:7 are directly adjacent with no digression between them, so this reads less like true Wiederaufnahme (resumption after interruption) and more like an ordinary vayehi-ki causal transition recapping the just-narrated cry to introduce Yahweh's response -- a common and unremarkable linking device in Hebrew narrative prose. I support disclosing the 6:6/6:7 echo, but would resolve it by naming it as a different category from the true resumption cases at 3:26/4:17 rather than assuming one of those two precedents must govern it.

First, the Hebrew citation for 7:4 fails character-for-character verification: the packet writes 'od with a telisha gedola on the ayin where MT points the word with a zinor after the dalet. This is the only accent substitution anywhere in the assigned range, and it is compounded by the fragment starting mid-verse, so that the verse's actual opening signal, the explicit-subject speech formula, never enters evidence at all. Second, the alternative the packet raises and rejects, closing at v7, turns out to be the reading both external witnesses support: WEB opens a paragraph before 7:8 and both parashah witnesses agree on a pe after 7:8, so the two marks bracket v8 at each end. MT also gives v8 its own fresh wayyiqtol with an explicit nominal subject, wayyiqchu et-tsedah ha-'am be-yadam. Markers cannot drive a boundary and, on a Prophets book, may never be treated as counter-evidence, so no boundary change is demanded; what is demanded is that the rejection stop being argued as though nothing outside the narrative logic bore on it. The seam is genuinely Janus-faced: v8 discharges v7's dismissal order, but it also introduces the trumpets the ambush needs and fixes the Midianite camp below Gideon for the night scene. Medium overstates a right edge that no witness supports and that the packet's own alternative already flagged as arguable; medium_low is the honest grade.

I verified that observation letter by letter and it is true: v23 and v24 both read wayyomer alehem gid'on, identical in wording, word order and explicit subject. But that is the campaign's own trigger for a reset, not for continuity. M8-Judg-125 states the rule explicitly, rejecting a merge because each round 'is introduced by its own fresh address paired with a distinct material and distinct outcome-language, an explicit-subject-reset-with-content-shift pattern treated as opening a new unit each time', and M8-Judg-001 likewise treats a speech-formula reset as a unit opener. Here the pattern is at its purest: the formula is not merely similar but identical, the subject is re-named although no participant has intervened, and the content shift is maximal, from refusing dynastic rule to soliciting gold. The alternative the packet names is therefore the one its own principle selects, and it is dismissed on a thematic ground, that the juxtaposition is the passage's literary point, when the governing rule is that text signals drive. There is one real defence, and the packet does not use it: WEB places no paragraph between v23 and v24 while paragraphing before v23 and again before v25, so the translation does tie the two speeches together. Medium is too generous while the seam is argued away thematically.

primary_reviews.rationale: Both edges hold and the error is in the description of the interior. v34 carries out the night ambush in four companies, converting Zebul's plan into action, with a WEB paragraph; v38 ends on the goading imperative tse na attah we-hillachem bo, and v39 has Gaal actually go out and fight, with both parashah witnesses agreeing on a samekh after 9:38. Splitting the positioning from the dialogue is properly refused, since the dialogue's tension depends on the ambush already being in place. But the account of what passes between the two men reverses their roles. The packet has Gaal 'progressively misreading the approaching troops, first as shadows, then as real companies, each round punctuated by Zebul's mounting sarcasm'. In MT it is Zebul who introduces shadows, at v36, in order to talk Gaal out of what Gaal has correctly seen; Gaal never misreads anything, identifying descending troops accurately at v36 and again at v37. Nor is Zebul's first reply sarcasm: he is Abimelech's inside man, he summoned the ambush himself at v31, and the shadows line buys time. Only at v38 does he drop the pretence. Reversing the agency converts the scene's engine, an insider stalling until the trap closes, into an ordinary case of a braggart's confusion. primary_reviews.rationale: Opening edge at v4 is a clean speech-to-action pivot off the grievance dialogue closed at 12:3 (decision 096, adjacent cluster) - Jephthah stops answering and starts mustering, a subject-verb reset with a named actor. Closing edge at v6 lands on the casualty tally, and v7's tenure-and-death notice is a total register change (battle report to obituary formula), so both edges hold. The considered split (battle proper v4 vs. checkpoint vv5-6) fails on its own merits: the fords-seizure in v5 has no new subject or scene marker, it is the same Gileadite militia continuing the same engagement, so keeping it fused is correct. Both oshb and web citations verified against source text at Judg.12.4 and Judg.12.6; casualty figure and Shibboleth wording match. This is the correct call on the focus-test question of whether 12:1-6 was fused: it was not. The campaign split the intertribal-threat speech (12:1-3) from the muster-and-battle (12:4-6) on a genuine dialogue-to-combat boundary, the same class of signal used for the Ephraim-vs-Gideon parallel at 8:1-3 and for the vow-to-battle seam at 11:31/32. Treating the checkpoint scene as the battle's own resolution rather than a separate episode is sound narrative logic - a dialect-test ambush at a river crossing is the mechanism of the pursuit, not a second engagement.

The second alternative is a genuine contribution rather than a restatement of the adopted span, and its comparison holds up. The two Ephraimite quarrels really are a structural family — each opens with a grievance framed as a question and answered by the judge in the first person — and the divergence identified is the right one: the earlier episode resolves entirely inside Gideon's placating speech and moves straight on to his own pursuit at 8:4, with no battle against Ephraim following, whereas 12:3 ends on Jephthah's own unanswered question about being fought against, which 12:4 answers by mustering Gilead and doing exactly that. Cousins in form, not twins in outcome, is a fair summary. The parashah disclosure is honest and correct: chapter 12's marks are petuchot after 12:7, 12:10, 12:12 and 12:15 with no setumot at all, so nothing arbitrates the 12:3 seam. One citation note: the 12:3 fragment is printed with the non-pausal vocalization that belongs to 12:1, not with the pausal form the stored line carries at 12:3; the shared root that carries the argument is unaffected.

Single-verse unit; opening and closing coincide with the verse boundary. Attaching this verse to 097 as its coda was rightly rejected - a tenure-death notice is not narrative continuation of a battle, it is the hero-cycle's standard closing colophon, and folding it into the preceding action would blur a formula this campaign otherwise isolates consistently. Hebrew and WEB text confirmed verbatim; the cross-reference to Othniel (3:11), Ehud (3:30), and Gideon (8:28) as parallel treatments is consistent with how this genre of closing formula behaves across the book. This is clean hero-cycle closure grammar: name, verb of judging, duration, death, burial site, in that fixed order, functioning exactly like a colophon on a tablet. High confidence is earned here - both edges are formula-driven, not paragraph-driven or inferential.

Isolating 12:7 is right, and the grade survives scrutiny: a paragraph opens at 12:7 and another at 12:8, with the agreed pe after 12:7 between them, so both edges have external support and HIGH stands. primary_reviews.rationale: Opens on the same succession formula, closes on the same death-burial formula; both edges present despite the entry's brevity. This is the sharpest test of the focus question, since Elon's entry carries no unique anecdote at all - no sons, no distinguishing detail, just the tenure figure. The rejected alternative (folding Elon into Ibzan's span) is nonetheless correctly rejected: what differentiates Elon is the explicit-subject formula-reset itself, which m8-mesh-r2 names as a governing principle in its own right, not a fallback used only when content differentiation runs out. A bare formula reset is a text signal here, not the prohibited marker-only case (that prohibition targets paratextual marks like pilcrows or petuchah/samekh used alone, not a repeated Hebrew narrative formula). Hebrew and WEB wording for v11-12 matches source exactly, including the double mention of the ten-year tenure. This is the weakest-content entry in the register and the decision knows it - confidence is appropriately held at medium rather than inflated to match its siblings. I would not raise it further, but I would not lower it either; the formula-reset argument is sufficient on its own terms.

The explanation of the doubled judging-formula is a genuine insight and worth keeping: Elon's entry has no middle verse of independent content, unlike Ibzan's daughters or Abdon's donkey-riding sons, so the succession notice and the tenure notice are compressed into one verse and end up sharing its opening verb. Reading that as a structural consequence of brevity rather than as emphasis is right, and it also answers the merge alternative, since brevity does not deprive the entry of its own opening formula or its own burial closure. The grading defect is the same one that afflicts its neighbour, and it is independently present here.

The rationale only tests folding this verse into 116 (as arson's consequence) and rejects that. It does not test the mirror alternative - folding it into 118 as that unit's opening premise - even though 118's own rationale explicitly says Samson's vow 'directly respond[s] to the wife and father's murder just narrated,' i.e., treats v6 as its trigger. This campaign has already established a precedent for exactly this move: decision M8-Judg-092 (Judg.11.28-31, outside this cluster but reviewed for context) folds a bare failure-notice into the following unit as its 'opening premise' on the grounds that it is 'the direct hinge triggering the following action in the same causal breath.' Judg.15.6 fits that same description for 118 at least as well as it fits standing alone. The single-verse scope is honestly flagged as tempering confidence, but the alternative that was actually tested is the weaker of the two available alternatives. Hebrew and WEB text for 15:6 verified accurately against source; no citation error here, this is a structural-consistency question, not a factual one. I am not asserting the boundary is wrong - isolating a dual-attaching bridge verse as its own unit is a defensible middle path and arguably the most neutral option precisely because it can be read either direction. But the stated rejected-alternative testing is incomplete against the campaign's own internal precedent, and a fuller test that also weighed folding into 118 would either strengthen this decision's case or surface a real alternative worth adjudicating.

primary_reviews.rationale: Discounting the mid-story notice in favour of 16:31 alone was correctly refused. The verse stands at a genuine narrative pause and suppressing it would resolve by omission the very doubling the campaign is meant to disclose.

Single verse, tenure-closing formula. Opens on a hard register break from the spring-etiology's narrative mode into bare notice; closes at the verse boundary itself, and 16:1's Gaza scene begins with no lexical or narrative bridge back to Lehi. Discounting this occurrence as redundant with 16:31 and reassigning the 'real' close to the death-notice was considered and rightly rejected. This is the strongest call in the cluster and goes directly to the focus-test question of whether 15:20 closes a genuine narrative unit, forming two panels with ch16. It does: chs 13-15 form a complete arc (birth, marriage-and-Timnah, revenge-and-Lehi) with its own set of characters, locations, and escalating conflict with the Timnite in-laws, entirely resolved by 15:17-19. Ch16 opens a wholly new complex (Gaza, then Delilah) with no returning characters except Samson himself. The doubled colophon is not redundancy - it is the seam marker for a genuine two-panel structure, and disclosing rather than resolving it is the methodologically correct choice. Hebrew for 15:20 verified verbatim against source; wording is identical in structure to 16:31's close ('he judged Israel... years'), confirming the doubling claim is accurate, not overstated. This is well-recognized in Judges scholarship as a genuine structural crux, and the decision's choice to treat it as a disclosed, deliberate doubling rather than smoothing it into a single notice is the defensible position - it matches how a diplomatic-correspondence-trained eye would treat two authenticating seals on two separate documents rather than assume a scribal accident.

primary_reviews.rationale: This is where the decision goes wrong. The draft considers merging rounds three and four and rejects it because 'v13-14's material is formally still a deceptive half-truth', a content argument. primary_reviews.rationale: The formal move is honest as far as it goes -- conceding that the explicit-subject-reset criterion does not separate round three from round four, and stating a different ground, register-closure, instead of quietly overriding the criterion, is the right kind of transparency. But the register-closure argument itself does not hold up as cleanly as it is presented. It calls rounds one through three uniform half-truths narrated at the same distance, but round three's own opening line, ad hennah hetalta bi, until now you have mocked me, repeats round two's accusation, hinneh hetalta bi vatedabberi elai kezavim, almost word for word, and round four's opening line explicitly counts back to it: zeh shalosh pe'amim hetalta bi, these three times you have mocked me. That is the same root, the same accusation, carried straight across the seam the row says marks a qualitative break in kind. The four rounds read less like three matched half-truths followed by one register-different escalation, and more like an accusation that starts at round two, repeats at round three, and gets tallied and intensified at round four -- a continuous crescendo, not a clean two-part structure. The seam might still be defensible on other grounds, but as stated, the argument omits the very textual thread that would need to be addressed to make it.

challenges.claim: The register-closure argument for keeping the 16:14/16:15 seam describes rounds one through three as uniform 'half-truths... narrated at the same distance' against round four's 'qualitative break in kind,' but round three's own accusation (Judg.16.13, ad hennah hetalta bi) already repeats round two's wording (Judg.16.10, hinneh hetalta bi vatedabberi elai kezavim) almost verbatim, and round four's opening (Judg.16.15, zeh shalosh pe'amim hetalta bi) explicitly tallies back across that same root rather than introducing a new one -- a continuity the rationale does not address.
challenges.suggested_action: Either acknowledge the hetalta-bi thread running from round two through round four and re-argue why round four still constitutes a distinct register rather than an intensification of an already-present accusation, or reconsider whether the 16:14/16:15 seam is better described as the weakest of the four round-boundaries rather than one resting on a clean content break.

primary_reviews.rationale: Single verse combining burial notice and the second tenure-formula. Opens on a register shift to the brothers' calm recovery of the body, closes at the verse boundary; ch17 opens the appendices with no framework formula at all, a total register change (no more judge-cycle grammar of any kind). Downgrading 15:20 to a mere aside and treating only this verse as the 'real' close was rightly rejected, and the inverse move (treating only 15:20 as real) was equally avoidable - both notices use identical closing vocabulary and both sit at genuine narrative pauses, so this decision's parity with 122 is the methodologically consistent choice. This directly answers the focus-test question: yes, 15:20 closes a genuine mid-cycle unit, and chs 13-15 / ch16 do function as two panels, each sealed by its own occurrence of the identical tenure-formula. Hebrew for 16:31 verified verbatim against source, including the tenure clause's exact wording match to 15:20 ('he judged Israel twenty years'), confirming the doubling is a precise verbal repetition, not an approximate echo. Together, 122 and 134 form the cleanest piece of hero-cycle closure grammar in this entire assigned range: a doubled colophon disclosed rather than resolved, treated with identical methodology at both occurrences, each with independent narrative-pause support on its own side of the seam. This is the strongest structural call in clusters 13-17.

The corrected comparison is accurate against both verses and both citations match the stored lines exactly. The mid-career notice uses a wayyiqtol with no independent subject and adds the phrase about the days of the Philistines; the death notice fronts an independent pronoun before a qatal and omits that phrase; and the shared material really is limited to the object phrase, the numeral and the verbal root. The inference drawn from that is the part I find genuinely strengthening rather than defensive: two structurally different colophon constructions bracketing one twenty-year figure is harder to explain as scribal duplication than two identical notices would be, so the morphosyntactic contrast argues for a deliberate two-panel frame instead of weakening the doubling disclosure. The grade holds, with paragraphs opening at 16:31 and at 17:1 and the agreed mark after 16:31 between them, and the alternative rightly refuses to privilege one notice over the other, since suppressing either would hide the doubling this decision exists to surface.

primary_reviews.rationale: The factual correction is right and worth crediting -- the two tenure notices really do differ in verb form, in the presence of an independent subject pronoun, and in whether days of the Philistines is attached, and the old identical-closing-vocabulary claim was simply wrong. But the new argument built on top of that correction overreaches: it says the morphosyntactic contrast is harder to explain as accidental scribal duplication than two verbatim-identical notices would be, and treats that as itself evidence for deliberate two-panel composition. I do not think that direction of inference holds up, and this book supplies its own counter-example: where this campaign's own evidence treats a doubling as a genuine, deliberate literary bracket, the 17:6/21:25 refrain, it is because the two instances are byte-identical, not because they diverge. Divergent doublets are, if anything, more often read as evidence of two source-strands awkwardly retained than as a considered stylistic device. The disclosure itself, two tenure notices exist and here is how they differ, is honest and sufficient; the causal claim riding on top of it is not earned by anything in the record.

challenges.claim: The corrected rationale asserts that the morphosyntactic contrast between the two Samson tenure-notices (Judg.15.20, wayyiqtol, no subject pronoun, plus 'days of the Philistines'; Judg.16.31, fronted pronoun plus qatal, no such phrase) is 'harder to explain as accidental scribal duplication... than two verbatim-identical notices would be' and treats this as evidence of a deliberate 'two-panel composition.' This inference is not supported in the record and runs against this book's own comparandum: the refrain this campaign already treats as a deliberate literary bracket (Judg.17.6/21.25) is byte-identical, not divergent, which is the more usual signature of an intentional inclusio.
challenges.suggested_action: Keep the corrected factual comparison of the two tenure notices, but drop or soften the claim that their divergence is itself evidence of deliberate two-panel design; disclosing the doubling and its actual wording difference is sufficient without the added causal inference.

primary_reviews.rationale: Reading the refrain as the opener of 17:7-13 was correctly refused. Beyond the form argument, 17:7 supplies its own presentative opener, so the refrain would be redundant as an opener and has no such competition as a closer.

Opens on the static shrine inventory, closes on the full two-clause refrain. v7 opens an entirely new character (the wandering Levite), a hard cast-and-topic change. Reading the refrain as opening the Levite narrative (matching its short-form function at 18:1/19:1) was rightly rejected. Checked directly against source: 18:1 reads only 'In those days there was no king in Israel' before pivoting immediately to unrelated content (the Danites seeking territory), and 19:1 reads only 'In those days, when there was no king in Israel' before introducing the Levite-and-concubine narrative - neither carries the second clause. 17:6 and 21:25, by contrast, both carry the full two-clause form verbatim ('...Everyone did that which was right in his own eyes'), confirmed by direct comparison of the two verses, which are word-for-word identical. This is a genuine, verifiable inclusio bracketing the entire appendix (chs 17-21) with matching closing formulas, while the short one-clause form does separate, lighter opening duty at each internal narrative pivot. All four comparison verses (17:6, 18:1, 19:1, 21:25) checked directly against Judg_web_clean.txt; the short-form/full-form distinction claimed in the rationale is factually accurate in every instance, not an approximation. This is the strongest single factual claim tested anywhere in my assigned range, and it holds up completely: a real, verified verbal inclusio (17:6...21:25) correctly used to justify treating the full refrain as a closing bracket rather than an opener. Worth noting for the record that this unit's near edge (v6) sits inside a single unbroken WEB paragraph that WEB itself continues straight through v7 without a pilcrow - so this boundary is being set entirely by the disclosed short-form/full-form distinction, not by any inherited paragraph break, which is about as clean an answer to the 'rides a WEB paragraph' focus test as this range offers.

I also confirmed the setumah after 18:1 is real (it is in the samekh list of parashah_two_witness.json). Where I differ slightly from OL: of the two remedies on offer, I would not push toward merging 138 into 139 through the oracle at 18:6. Decision 139's own opening (the voice-recognition at 18:3) is a genuine scene-trigger in its own right, distinct from the mere arrival-and-lodging notice that closes 18:2, and collapsing that distinction loses information the campaign elsewhere protects (compare how carefully 140/141 separate narration from report by register). primary_reviews.rationale: The compound-closure reading itself is sound - v30 and v31 do supply two distinct, parallel duration-formulas (עַד י֖וֹם גְּל֥וֹת הָאָֽרֶץ and כָּל יְמֵ֛י הֱי֥וֹת בֵּית הָאֱלֹהִ֖ים בְּשִׁלֹֽה, both verified verbatim), and the pe recorded after 18:31 correctly matches this decision's own closing edge. The oshb ketiv at v30 reads בֶּ֣ן מְנַשֶּׁ֜ה - 'son of Manasseh' - not Moses; this is the famous suspended-nun site (b. Bava Batra 109b), where a nun was inserted into מֹשֶׁה to produce מְנַשֶּׁה specifically so the consonantal text would NOT plainly say a grandson of Moses served an idol. WEB's 'the son of Moses' follows the traditional qere/pronunciation, which is what actually discloses the shocking genealogy - the ketiv the decision itself quotes right alongside that WEB rendering is the smoothing-over device, not the disclosure. So the rationale has the two textual layers reversed: the printed consonants smooth it over, the traditional reading discloses it, not the other way around.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: This is the cluster's blind-convergence case and I re-derived it independently before reading either primary's challenge language closely. Judg.18.30 as printed in the source reads בֶּן מְנַשֶּׁ֜ה - Manasseh - and only that form; there is no bracketed alternate spelling the way 19:3's off-glossed pronoun shows a plain ketiv form sitting beside a pointed qere form. Bava Batra 109b; the extra nun inserted into what would otherwise read Mosheh), which both primaries correctly identify in substance even though 'ketiv/qere inversion' is a slightly loose label for it - the nun-suspension is its own category of Masoretic apparatus, distinct from a regular two-form ketiv/qere dyad, though it functions the same way for this decision's purposes (the plain consonantal text reads one thing, the received tradition and WEB read another). Whichever label is used, the direction the decision draws is backwards: the printed form is the smoothing device, and the traditional reading WEB follows is what discloses the Mosaic line serving an idol at the book's structural hinge. Both primaries reach this independently without having seen each other's work, which is the strongest kind of corroboration this campaign's rules recognize. I confirm the challenge and support the remedy both primaries converge on: state the divergence rather than resolve it silently, and correct 'disclosed here rather than smoothed over' to reflect which layer does which.

primary_reviews.rationale: Verifying that 19:1's refrain is a third, distinct construction, wayehi-prefixed, word order inverted, genuinely different from both 18:1's adverbial repetition and 17:6/21:25's plain form, rather than assimilating it to 18:1's fix by analogy, is the more careful move, and the byte-comparison backing it up is the right kind of check. peer_crosscheck.assessment: I pulled all four refrain instances directly rather than trusting any single citation: Judg.17.6 and Judg.21.25 are an exact NFC-normalized match, character for character including every cantillation mark - true byte-identity, not an approximation. Judg.18.1's first clause, בַּיָּמִ֣ים הָהֵ֔ם אֵ֥ין מֶ֖לֶךְ בְּיִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל, is also an exact match to that same string. Judg.19.1 is not: it reads וַיְהִי֙ בַּיָּמִ֣ים הָהֵ֔ם וּמֶ֖לֶךְ אֵ֣ין בְּיִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל - prefixed by a wayehi that neither 17:6/21:25 nor 18:1 carries, and with the king/negation order inverted (king-then-negation instead of negation-then-king). That means there are three distinct grammatical strategies in play across the book's four refrain instances, not one 'short form' treated identically at both its outings as the decision claims. The high confidence rating and the 'for the identical reason given' cross-reference to 138 cannot both stand once 19:1's actual construction is checked against 18:1's. I also confirm OL's smaller, correctly-flagged point: the WEB gloss 'to bring her again' at 19:3 follows the qere לַהֲשִׁיבָ֔הּ against the ketiv להשיבו, which the source shows printed as an explicit ketiv-then-qere pair (unlike 147's suspended nun, this is the standard two-form apparatus) and which the decision's rationale silently adopts without disclosure.

challenges.claim: Two problems. First, the row states flatly that the host is 'the grammatical subject of both verbs' in v25. The noun is not disambiguated in the Hebrew — the same designation is used for the guest throughout the chapter and for the householder in vv22-23 — and the possessive on the object phrase points to the Levite, whose concubine she is, not to the host. The overstatement replaces one unsupported reading with another in the opposite direction. evidence: oshb:Judg.1.2 וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יְהוָ֖ה יְהוּדָ֣ה יַעֲלֶ֑ה הִנֵּ֛ה נָתַ֥תִּי אֶת הָאָ֖רֶץ בְּיָדֽוֹ — the answer at the book's opening is 'Judah shall go up', with a land-grant clause attached.

בַּתְּחִלָּה occurs in the question at 1:1 and migrates into the answer at 20:18; that migration is itself the interesting datum, and the decision loses it by asserting identity instead.
Secondary: the inquiry verbs differ in their complement — 1:1 וַֽיִּשְׁאֲלוּ֙ ... בַּיהוָ֖ה against 20:18 וַיִּשְׁאֲל֣וּ בֵאלֹהִים֒ — and 20:18 adds a sanctuary location (בֵֽית אֵל֮) that 1:1 lacks.

Secondary: 'inclusio' is imprecise for a device whose second member stands at 20:18 with a further chapter and the book's own closing refrain still to come. A resumptive frame around chs 1-20 is what the evidence shows.

primary_reviews.rationale: This is a strong, well-formed single-verse decision with clean edges on both sides (troop-count register giving way to cultic inquiry, then inquiry giving way to fresh muster notice), and the book-spanning inclusio with 1:1-2 is real: מִ֚י יַעֲלֶה לָּ֣נוּ...בַּתְּחִלָּ֔ה genuinely reuses 1:1's own מִ֣י יַעֲלֶה לָּ֧נוּ...בַּתְּחִלָּ֖ה almost clause for clause, an unmistakable and pointed echo turning the conquest-opening formula into a civil-war formula. primary_reviews.rationale: The precision repair is exactly right and I checked both halves of it against the two verses. The question-formula does recur near-verbatim across the book's two ends, differing only in the object of the campaign and in one prepositional detail, while the answers share nothing beyond the tribe's name and the divine-speech opener: the opening oracle answers with a verb plus an attached land-grant clause, whereas the closing one drops the verb and migrates the adverb out of the question into the answer. Downgrading the claim from a verbatim doubling of the whole exchange to a resumptive echo concentrated in the question is the accurate description, and the ironic structural point — a civil war against a fellow tribe framed by the conquest-opening inquiry — survives the correction intact, which is what makes this a strengthening rather than a retreat. The grade holds on the both-edges test, with paragraphs opening at both 20:18 and 20:19, and the alternative rightly separates a cultic act from the numerical muster-register that precedes it.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: This is the range's second headline blind-convergence and I re-derived it from scratch before comparing notes with either primary's challenge text. Pulled all three verses fresh: Judg.1.1 מִ֣י יַעֲלֶה לָּ֧נוּ אֶל הַֽכְּנַעֲנִ֛י בַּתְּחִלָּ֖ה, Judg.1.2 וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יְהוָ֖ה יְהוּדָ֣ה יַעֲלֶ֑ה הִנֵּ֛ה נָתַ֥תִּי אֶת הָאָ֖רֶץ בְּיָדֽוֹ, Judg.20.18 מִ֚י יַעֲלֶה לָּ֣נוּ בַתְּחִלָּ֔ה לַמִּלְחָמָ֖ה עִם בְּנֵ֣י בִנְיָמִ֑ן וַיֹּ֥אמֶר יְהוָ֖ה יְהוּדָ֥ה בַתְּחִלָּֽה. The question-formula echo is genuinely close to verbatim (mi ya'aleh lanu...ba-techillah recurs almost clause for clause). The answer is not: 1:2 gives יְהוּדָ֣ה יַעֲלֶ֑ה plus an attached land-grant clause, while 20:18 gives the shorter יְהוּדָ֥ה בַתְּחִלָּֽה, borrowing its own verb-substitute from the question rather than repeating 1:2's יַעֲלֶה. 'Judah first' as an English quotation is accurate only for 20:18; rendering 1:2's answer that way, or calling the two answers 'identical,' overstates the match. Both primaries caught this independently in a genuinely blind pass, which is the strongest form of corroboration under this campaign's rules. I also note an earlier-cluster digest entry (OL-M8-Judg-001-1, filed against decision 1 at Judg.1.1-1.2) asserts the recurrence is 'verbatim...for all three elements' including 'the answer wayyomer YHWH Yehudah' - read narrowly, that claim is defensible (the introductory 'and Yahweh said, Judah' clause-opener is shared), but it should not be stretched to cover the full answers, which diverge exactly where this decision's language claims they don't. I support both primaries' proposed correction: relocate the verbatim claim to the question-formula and the migration of ba-techillah from question to answer, and treat 'inclusio' as a resumptive frame given the book's own closing refrain still lies ahead of 20:18.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: This is the range's third resumption-cut dispute and I checked it with the same rigor as 18:17/18:18 and 20:45/20:47, and it lands differently. Judg.21.5 reads מִ֠י אֲשֶׁ֨ר לֹא עָלָ֧ה בַקָּהָ֛ל מִכָּל שִׁבְטֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל אֶל יְהוָ֑ה, and Judg.21.8 reads מִ֗י אֶחָד֙ מִשִּׁבְטֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אֲשֶׁ֛ר לֹֽא עָלָ֥ה אֶל יְהוָ֖ה הַמִּצְפָּ֑ה. These share the interrogative, the negated verb of going up, the tribal phrase, and the divine name, but the word order and the surrounding phrasing differ - this is lexical and thematic resumption (the suspended question being picked back up), not the byte-identical clause repetition verified at the other two headline seams. I want to be precise about that distinction so the campaign does not treat all three seams as the same strength of evidence: 18:17/18:18 and 20:45/20:47 are Wiederaufnahme in the strict philological sense; 21:5/21:8 is closer to a resumed topic using overlapping vocabulary. That said, the substantive point behind the challenge does not depend on the strict form - I confirmed the מוֹת יוּמָת death-penalty clause sits at 21:5, which is inside this decision's own drafted span (21:4-21:7), while decision 170 treats that same clause as 'the earlier Mizpah oath's own built-in penalty clause' as though it belonged to a prior, separate unit. That is a genuine internal inconsistency between the two decisions' own argumentation, independent of how strong the resumption device itself is. I support re-closing 169 at 21:4 and opening the enquiry-to-solution unit at 21:5 running through 21:12, per OL's proposal, on the strength of that inconsistency rather than purely on the resumption argument.

primary_reviews.rationale: Three checkable claims here, and all three survive independent testing. The elders of the congregation are named as speakers only at 21:16 in this book, so the opening reset is as distinctive as the row says. The cursing root occurs only at 5:23 and here — the similar-looking forms at 16:13 and 20:27 belong to unrelated roots — so the contrast between an imperative with an infinitive absolute there and a passive participle here is precisely drawn rather than loosely gestured at. And 21:19 does open with no expressed subject, continuing the elders by inflection just as the preceding verse does, which is what forced the withdrawal of the 'new speaker' ground for the closing edge. Replacing it with a content shift, from restating the constraint to proposing a way around it, plus the setumah after 21:18, is the honest repair. The observation that the curse-formula recasts the oath of 21:1 without quoting it is also accurate: different verb, different construction, same substance. primary_reviews.rationale: Both corrections are real: v18's curse-formula is a recasting of the oath's substance, not a verbatim quotation of it, and v19 continues the same elders by inflection rather than introducing a new speaker. Relocating the boundary's actual basis to the content shift, restating the constraint versus proposing a way around it, is a legitimate rhetorical-function distinction even without a change of speaker, and it is a more honest ground than the false claim it replaces.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: Both primaries file independent, non-overlapping challenges against this same decision and both check out. On the opening side, LF is right that v18's אָר֕וּר נֹתֵ֥ן אִשָּׁ֖ה לְבִנְיָמִֽן is not a verbatim quotation of v1's אִ֣ישׁ מִמֶּ֔נּוּ לֹא יִתֵּ֥ן בִּתּ֛וֹ לְבִנְיָמִ֖ן לְאִשָּֽׁה - different verb, different construction, a curse-formula recasting rather than a repetition. On the closing side, OL is right that v19's וַיֹּאמְר֡וּ has no expressed subject and simply continues the elders introduced at v16 by inflection, exactly as v17's וַיֹּ֣אמְר֔וּ does - there is no 'new speaker' at v19, and the actual shift is one of content (restatement of the constraint giving way to a proposed way around it). I ran my own independent check the primaries did not run: a full-book search for the root ARR (curse) across Judg_oshb.txt. It occurs in exactly two places - here at 21:18, and at 5:23 in the Song of Deborah ('Curse Meroz,' said the angel of Yahweh...curse bitterly its inhabitants). Those two verses share the same three root consonants but not the same vocalization or grammatical function: 5:23 uses an imperative plus infinitive-absolute pair (אֹ֥רוּ...אָר֖וֹר, an intensifying 'utterly curse' construction), while 21:18 uses the Qal passive participle as a predicate (אָר֕וּר, 'cursed is...'). LF's claim that the specific participial form אָרוּר used as a predicate is unique to 21:18 remains correct once this distinction is drawn, but the bare claim 'occurs exactly once in the entire book' is imprecise about the consonantal root versus the specific form, and I recommend tightening the language to specify the predicate-participle usage rather than the root.
